items.title: Lifetime Heartwork
items.question: Estimate a person's lifetime heartbeats using 70 beats per minute and an 80-year life. Which order of magnitude is closest?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 70 x 60 x 24 x 365 x 80 is about 2.9 billion beats.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 3 billion. Round 70 beats per minute to 100 and 80 years to 100 for a quick upper estimate, then refine to land near three billion.
items.lessonContent:
Fermi estimates multiply a rate by the time over which it acts.
Round first so the arithmetic stays visible, then refine the largest assumption.
An answer within a factor of two is often enough to reveal the correct scale.
Writing units beside each factor catches missing minutes, days, or years.
Share this: estimate your own lifetime heartbeat count from your resting pulse.

items.title: Breaths by Bedtime
items.question: A resting adult takes about 15 breaths per minute. Roughly how many breaths is that in one day?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 15 x 60 x 24 equals 21,600, so twenty thousand is the useful estimate.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 20,000. Fifteen breaths each minute becomes about 900 an hour, then roughly 21,600 across a day.
items.lessonContent:
Convert a per-minute rate to a daily total in two steps: minutes to hours, then hours to days.
Round after the multiplication, not before every small factor.
A sanity check can compare breathing rate with a familiar clock rhythm.
Estimates describe scale rather than pretending measurements are exact.
Share this: count one quiet minute of breathing and project it across tomorrow.

items.title: Faucet in a Day
items.question: A dripping faucet loses one 0.25-millilitre drop each second. Roughly how many litres does it waste per day?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 0.25 millilitres x 86,400 seconds is 21.6 litres, close to twenty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 20 litres. Four drops make one millilitre, so 86,400 daily drops become 21,600 millilitres, or about twenty litres.
items.lessonContent:
Tiny rates become large totals when time supplies enough repetitions.
Convert millilitres to litres only after building the daily volume.
Grouping four quarter-millilitre drops into one millilitre simplifies the arithmetic.
A result should be checked against a bucket-sized physical reference.
Share this: time a real leak for one minute and estimate its daily waste.

items.title: Shower Tank Test
items.question: A shower flows at 9 litres per minute. About how much water does an 8-minute shower use?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 9 x 8 is 72 litres, which rounds cleanly to about seventy.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 70 litres. Multiplying flow rate by duration gives 72 litres, and the input rate was approximate anyway.
items.lessonContent:
Volume equals flow rate multiplied by elapsed time.
Approximate inputs do not justify falsely precise outputs.
Rounding 9 to 10 gives a quick upper check before doing the closer multiplication.
Household resource use becomes tangible when converted into container-sized totals.
Share this: time tomorrow's shower and estimate the volume before leaving the bathroom.

items.title: Classroom Air
items.question: A classroom is 10 m long, 8 m wide, and 3 m high. Roughly what volume of air does it contain?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - treating the room as a box gives 10 x 8 x 3 = 240 cubic metres.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 240 cubic metres. A box model ignores furniture and people but captures the room's air volume at the right scale.
items.lessonContent:
Complicated spaces can often be replaced by boxes, cylinders, or spheres.
A useful model keeps the dimensions that dominate and ignores small obstructions.
Multiplying three lengths produces volume, so the unit must become cubic metres.
Geometry estimates are strongest when their simplifying shape is stated openly.
Share this: estimate the air volume of the room you are in using paced lengths.

items.title: Oxygen in the Room
items.question: Air is about 20% oxygen. If a room contains 240 cubic metres of air, roughly how many cubic metres are oxygen?
items.correctExplanation: Right - one fifth of 240 is 48 cubic metres, which is about fifty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 50 cubic metres. Replacing twenty percent with one fifth turns the calculation into 240 divided by five, or 48.
items.lessonContent:
Friendly fractions make percentage estimates fast: 20% is one fifth.
Use the fraction only when its approximation is accurate enough for the question.
A component volume equals the total volume multiplied by its fraction.
Round the result to match the roughness of the original proportion.
Share this: estimate how much oxygen occupies your bedroom before looking up its dimensions.

items.title: Raindrop Reservoir
items.question: A 10-millimetre rainstorm falls on a flat 100-square-metre roof. About how many litres of water land there?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 10 millimetres is 0.01 metre, and 0.01 x 100 makes one cubic metre, or 1,000 litres.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 1,000 litres. Rain depth multiplied by catchment area gives one cubic metre, and each cubic metre holds one thousand litres.
items.lessonContent:
Rainfall depth becomes volume when multiplied by the area receiving it.
Convert millimetres to metres before multiplying by square metres.
One cubic metre equals one thousand litres, a valuable bridge between geometry and daily life.
Thin layers over broad areas hide surprisingly large volumes.
Share this: estimate what your roof could collect from the next centimetre of rain.

items.title: Laptop Year
items.question: A laptop draws 50 watts for 8 hours each day. Roughly how much electrical energy does it use in a year?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 0.05 kilowatts x 8 hours x 365 days is about 146 kilowatt-hours.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 150 kilowatt-hours. Convert 50 watts to 0.05 kilowatts, multiply by eight daily hours, then by 365 days.
items.lessonContent:
Electrical energy equals power multiplied by time.
Convert watts to kilowatts before using billing units of kilowatt-hours.
Daily energy can be annualized by multiplying by roughly 365.
Keep power and energy distinct: watts are a rate, kilowatt-hours are a total.
Share this: estimate the annual energy of one device from its label and your usage.

items.title: Kettle Energy
items.question: A 2-kilowatt kettle runs for 3 minutes. About how much energy does one boil use in kilowatt-hours?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - three minutes is 0.05 hour, and 2 kilowatts x 0.05 hour equals 0.1 kilowatt-hour.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 0.1 kilowatt-hour. Convert three minutes to one twentieth of an hour, then multiply that duration by two kilowatts.
items.lessonContent:
Short appliance cycles require converting minutes into fractions of an hour.
Three minutes is one twentieth of an hour, a friendly fraction for mental arithmetic.
High power does not always mean high total energy when the runtime is brief.
Unit cancellation should leave kilowatt-hours, not kilowatts per hour.
Share this: estimate how many kettle boils make one kilowatt-hour.

items.title: Solar Roof Yield
items.question: A 5-kilowatt solar array averages 4 equivalent full-sun hours per day. Roughly how much energy does it produce daily?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 5 kilowatts x 4 sun-hours gives about 20 kilowatt-hours per day.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 20 kilowatt-hours. Equivalent sun-hours compress a variable day into four hours at the array's full rated power.
items.lessonContent:
Variable processes can be summarized with an equivalent full-rate duration.
Rated power multiplied by equivalent hours gives an energy estimate.
Weather, angle, and losses make the result a planning number rather than a guarantee.
State the assumed sun-hours because location can change them substantially.
Share this: estimate a nearby roof's daily solar yield from its panel count.

items.title: Elevator Trips
items.question: An elevator averages one trip every 2 minutes for 10 hours. Roughly how many trips does it make that day?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - ten hours contains 600 minutes, and one trip per two minutes gives 300 trips.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 300 trips. Convert ten hours to 600 minutes, then divide by the two-minute interval between trips.
items.lessonContent:
For repeating events, total count equals total time divided by time per event.
Division, not multiplication, is required when the given rate is minutes per trip.
Convert both quantities to the same time unit before combining them.
Check whether the result implies a plausible number of events per hour.
Share this: estimate today's elevator traffic while waiting for one ride.

items.title: Traffic Lane Flow
items.question: Cars pass a checkpoint every 2 seconds in one lane. Roughly how many cars pass in an hour?
items.correctExplanation: Right - an hour has 3,600 seconds, so one car every two seconds gives 1,800 cars.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 1,800 cars. Divide 3,600 seconds in an hour by the two seconds occupied by each passing interval.
items.lessonContent:
Flow can be estimated from the spacing between successive events.
A two-second headway means half an event per second.
Converting to an hourly rate makes transport capacities easier to compare.
Real congestion lowers the idealized rate through merging, braking, and uneven gaps.
Share this: count ten vehicle gaps and estimate the lane's hourly flow.

items.title: Walked in a Year
items.question: Someone walks 5,000 steps per day, averaging 0.8 metre per step. Roughly how far do they walk in a year?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 5,000 x 0.8 is 4 kilometres daily, or about 1,460 kilometres yearly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 1,500 kilometres. The daily distance is about four kilometres, and multiplying by 365 puts the annual total near fifteen hundred.
items.lessonContent:
Counts become distances when multiplied by an average length per event.
Convert metres to kilometres before annualizing to keep the numbers manageable.
An average stride is an assumption worth adjusting for the person being estimated.
A daily habit can accumulate to a cross-country scale over a year.
Share this: use your phone's step count to estimate last week's walking distance.

items.title: Earth Circumference Walk
items.question: Earth's circumference is about 40,000 km. At 20 km of walking per day, roughly how many years would one trip around take?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 40,000 divided by 20 is 2,000 walking days, or roughly five and a half years.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 5.5 years. The route requires 2,000 days at twenty kilometres daily, then dividing by 365 converts the total to years.
items.lessonContent:
Travel time equals distance divided by distance covered per day.
A daily rate can be converted into years after finding the total number of days.
Ignoring oceans and rest days defines an idealized lower bound.
Good estimates label such simplifications rather than hiding them.
Share this: estimate how long your usual daily walk would take to circle Earth.

items.title: Moon Signal Delay
items.question: The Moon is about 400,000 km away and radio travels near 300,000 km/s. Roughly how long is the one-way signal delay?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 400,000 divided by 300,000 is about 1.3 seconds one way.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 1.3 seconds. Dividing lunar distance by light speed gives four thirds of a second, while a reply would double the wait.
items.lessonContent:
Signal delay is distance divided by propagation speed.
Radio and light travel at essentially the same speed through space.
One-way and round-trip delays answer different operational questions.
Keeping both quantities in kilometres makes the units cancel cleanly.
Share this: pause for a lunar round trip before answering one message today.

items.title: Earth Data Loop
items.question: A fibre route around Earth is roughly 40,000 km, and signals in fibre move near 200,000 km/s. About how long is one loop?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 40,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.2 second, before routing and equipment delays.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 0.2 seconds. The path is one fifth of the distance the signal covers in a second, so propagation alone takes two tenths.
items.lessonContent:
Network latency has a physical floor set by path length and signal speed.
Light travels slower in glass than in vacuum.
Real routes are longer than map distances and add equipment delays at each hop.
Estimating the physical minimum helps separate unavoidable delay from poor engineering.
Share this: estimate the minimum delay to a city on the opposite side of Earth.

items.title: Phone Photo Hoard
items.question: A phone stores 10,000 photos averaging 3 megabytes each. Roughly how much storage do the photos occupy?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 10,000 x 3 megabytes is 30,000 megabytes, or roughly 30 gigabytes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 30 gigabytes. Multiply the average file size by the file count, then use about one thousand megabytes per gigabyte.
items.lessonContent:
Digital storage estimates multiply item count by average item size.
Powers of ten are usually sufficient when comparing storage plans.
Averages hide variation but still predict the total well across many files.
Convert units at the end so the intermediate multiplication remains simple.
Share this: estimate your photo library size before opening the storage settings.

items.title: Video Upload Wait
items.question: A 1-gigabyte video uploads at 10 megabits per second. Using 8 bits per byte, roughly how long should it take?
items.correctExplanation: Right - one gigabyte is about 8,000 megabits, and dividing by 10 gives 800 seconds, near 13 minutes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 13 minutes. Convert bytes to bits before dividing by the bit-rate, then convert roughly 800 seconds into minutes.
items.lessonContent:
Data size and data rate must use matching bit or byte units.
Eight bits per byte is the crucial conversion many quick estimates miss.
Transfer time equals total data divided by data per second.
Protocol overhead makes a measured upload slightly slower than the ideal result.
Share this: predict one upload's finish time from its size and the speed test result.

items.title: Stadium Crowd Mass
items.question: A stadium holds 50,000 people. At an average 70 kg per person, roughly what is the crowd's total mass?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 50,000 x 70 kg is 3.5 million kg, or 3,500 tonnes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 3,500 tonnes. Multiply head count by average body mass, then divide kilograms by one thousand to express tonnes.
items.lessonContent:
Population totals often come from count multiplied by an average per person.
Choose a rounded average that is plausible for the population being modelled.
Convert large kilogram totals to tonnes so the result is easier to picture.
The estimate can be bounded by trying lighter and heavier plausible averages.
Share this: estimate the total mass of the people in your next crowded venue.

items.title: Crowd Floor Space
items.question: At a dense but standing crowd of 2 people per square metre, about what area is needed for 10,000 people?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 10,000 people divided by 2 people per square metre gives 5,000 square metres.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 5,000 square metres. Area equals the number of people divided by the assumed crowd density.
items.lessonContent:
Density links a count to the space containing it.
When density is people per area, divide count by density to recover area.
Crowd-density assumptions strongly affect attendance estimates from photographs.
Trying two plausible densities provides a useful uncertainty range.
Share this: estimate the attendance of one public gathering from its area and spacing.

items.title: Coffee Bean Count
items.question: A coffee bean has a mass near 0.15 gram. Roughly how many beans are in a 1-kilogram bag?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 1,000 grams divided by 0.15 gram per bean is about 6,700, close to seven thousand.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 7,000 beans. Convert the bag to one thousand grams, then divide by the average mass of one bean.
items.lessonContent:
Object counts can be inferred from total mass divided by average mass per object.
Always convert the total and the sample into the same mass unit first.
A small measured sample can improve an estimate more than elaborate arithmetic.
Round the final count because natural objects vary in size.
Share this: weigh ten small objects and estimate how many fill their container.

items.title: Paper Stack Height
items.question: One sheet of office paper is about 0.1 millimetre thick. Roughly how tall is a stack of 10,000 sheets?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 10,000 x 0.1 millimetre is 1,000 millimetres, exactly one metre.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 1 metre. Multiplying ten thousand sheets by one tenth of a millimetre gives one thousand millimetres.
items.lessonContent:
Repeated microscopic thicknesses can build human-scale distances.
Multiply count by thickness before converting millimetres to metres.
Powers of ten make this kind of scale jump especially easy to audit.
A physical stack provides an intuitive check on an otherwise abstract count.
Share this: estimate the number of sheets in a visible paper stack from its height.

items.title: Bookcase Words
items.question: A shelf holds 40 books averaging 80,000 words each. Roughly how many words are on the shelf?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 40 x 80,000 is 3.2 million words, so three million captures the scale.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 3 million words. Four tens of books multiplied by eight tens of thousands of words produces a little over three million.
items.lessonContent:
Collection totals come from item count multiplied by a representative average.
Scientific notation or grouped powers of ten keep large products manageable.
The average should match the collection: novels, textbooks, and picture books differ.
A rough total is valuable even when individual items vary widely.
Share this: estimate the word count of one shelf before counting its books.

items.title: City Water Day
items.question: A city of 500,000 people uses about 150 litres of water per person daily. Roughly how much water is that each day?
items.correctExplanation: Right - 500,000 x 150 litres gives 75 million litres, or 75 megalitres each day.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 75 million litres. Multiply population by per-person use, keeping the three zeros in 150 separate until the end.
items.lessonContent:
City-scale resource demand is population multiplied by average demand per person.
Break awkward numbers into friendly factors to avoid calculator dependence.
Megalitres are often easier to interpret than tens of millions of litres.
Changing one per-person habit scales across every resident.
Share this: estimate your town's daily water use from its population.

items.title: Tree Carbon Year
items.question: If one mature tree absorbs roughly 20 kg of carbon dioxide per year, about how much do 500 trees absorb annually?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly - 500 x 20 kg is 10,000 kg, or about 10 tonnes per year.
items.incorrectExplanation: The estimate is 10 tonnes. Multiply the annual rate per tree by five hundred trees, then convert one thousand kilograms to each tonne.
items.lessonContent:
Environmental totals often scale a measured per-unit rate across many units.
Per-tree rates vary with species, age, climate, and measurement method.
The arithmetic may be simple while the uncertainty sits mainly in the assumption.
Report the result as an order-of-magnitude planning estimate, not a universal constant.
Share this: estimate the annual carbon uptake of the trees on your street.
